corrections.how: Start with Tony's own phone only. Install the App Store app and pair with a limited setup code (no administrative access on the phone). Two approvals follow: the device, then its declared command surface. Allowed for iOS by default: camera.list, location.get, device.info, device.status, contacts.search, calendar.events, reminders.list, photos.latest, motion.activity, motion.pedometer, system.notify, plus talk.ptt.* for a Talk-capable node. Give the nodes tool only to the agent that owns the phone. In the in-house before_tool_call hook, allow each agent an exact list of node id and action or command pairs and block everything else, including the tool's pending, approve and reject actions and its generic invoke for unlisted commands. Any other phone (Jordan's, or a spare) is a separate decision, because every iPhone setup code also hands the phone an operator session. A spare phone, if one is used, gets the voice-node profile, is not signed in to happy's Apple Account, and sits in Guided Access with Touch switched off. Idle on a charger: the full surface answers only while the app is open in the foreground (keep-awake setting on, Guided Access holding the app on screen). Every iPhone setup code carries an operator session as well as the node: full (admin), limited (approvals, read, write and Talk secrets) or voice-node (read and Talk). The app reports setup as incomplete without both credentials; a node-only code is documented only for the Apple Watch.
The docs table is the gateway's ceiling, not proof of what the App Store build declares.

Operator scopes are gateway-wide. OpenClaw says they are not isolation between people: read covers every agent's sessions and logs, write covers tool invocation and command relay to any node, and the app has an agent picker and a read-only browser of the selected agent's workspace. Pairing Jordan's phone would let it see Tony's agents, which conflicts with roadmap 1b (family members only chat).

The nodes tool has no per-agent node filter. It lists every paired node, and its actions include pending, approve, reject and a generic invoke. The in-house hook is the only thing keeping an agent on its owner's phone.
gateway.nodes.commands.allow and deny are global: a command enabled for one phone is enabled for every paired phone that declares it, and a deny removes it for all of them.

In the installed source a paired node can also start an agent turn by itself (agent.request and voice.transcript events) and names the session in its own payload. These are not tool calls, so a before_tool_call hook never sees them, and by my reading the same event can name a delivery channel and recipient, which the recipient-pin hook would not see either. Treat every paired phone as able to talk to any agent.
corrections.safety:
A node is a peripheral that adds sensors and personal data to whichever agent holds the nodes tool, so keep it off the research and mail-reader agents. A paired iPhone is also a control-plane client: its operator session is not limited to one person's agents. Only Tony's phone fits the roadmap as written; pairing any other phone is an explicit decision to let that phone read across agents. Each

-main may reach only that person's phone, enforced by the hook (exact node id and command allowlist, pairing actions blocked) rather than by prompt. Dangerous commands stay out of gateway.nodes.commands.allow until a specific feature needs one; camera.clip, screen.record, contacts.add, calendar.add and reminders.add go into gateway.nodes.commands.deny. A spare phone is never signed in to happy's Apple Account, and its device entry is revoked on the gateway if it leaves the house.

caveats: One Mac and one iPhone at a time, and the session ends as soon as someone unlocks the phone.
Mirroring pauses after inactivity and asks for Mac authentication unless set to authenticate automatically. A Mac mini has no built-in Touch ID, so an unattended agent can stall at that prompt.
No camera or microphone through mirroring, including Face ID, so any app step that wants a face scan or a camera scan is a dead end.
Control is by pixels: a screenshot per step, slow, and broken by every app redesign. The computer tool has no per-action confirmation.
Neither Apple nor OpenClaw documents this combination, and OpenClaw's iOS page says the iPhone app is not a computer-use backend.
It also turns the Mac's display into a working surface, which changes the current headless posture.

The computer tool is not limited to the iPhone Mirroring window. It sees and controls happy's whole desktop, and OpenClaw runs the driver unrestricted, with authorization only at the level of exposing the tool. Messages (Happy's iMessage identity), the logged-in session and the gateway's files are on that same desktop, so one bad click path goes around the recipient pin and the sandbox.
Once computer control is enabled, any gateway client with write scope can invoke it; there is no admin check per action.

Messages and Safari cannot be deleted from an iPhone in the US, so a mirrored phone always has a way to send data out, and its Settings app offers a path to change the password of the Apple Account that Happy's iMessage runs on (the Apple page I read does not say what it asks for first).

iPhones reboot themselves after about 72 hours without an unlock (reported by security researchers; Apple has not documented it). A spare phone that must stay locked for mirroring will run into this unless someone unlocks it by hand.
The Mac keeps a computer-use run awake for at most one hour and ends it when the screen locks.
corrections.safety: No safe placement found. The agent would touch all three trifecta legs at once (the phone's logged-in apps, whatever those apps show, and a screen that can post, browse or message), and tool policy cannot separate them. The same tool also reaches happy's Mac desktop, where Messages, the Keychain session and the gateway state live, with no per-app limit and no per-action confirmation. The phone-side limits do not hold either: Messages and Safari stay on the phone and Settings is reachable. A hook could only approve or block whole clicks without knowing what they hit. Recommendation: do not build on this host. If Tony wants to experiment, do it attended, under a different Mac user or on a machine that holds no family data.
unverified: That Peekaboo or the CUA driver can reliably click and type inside the iPhone Mirroring window.

corrections.how:
Phone to Happy: a personal automation in Shortcuts on the parent's phone, set to run without asking, whose action is Get Contents of URL with a POST to a gateway hook over the tailnet. On the gateway: hooks.enabled, a dedicated hooks.token, hooks.allowedAgentIds limited to one new 'events' agent that has no tools and no memory (never a

-main or

-jobs agent), and a hooks.mappings entry per event id whose action is an isolated agent turn with fixed text; code then delivers the fixed result to the owner. Because the one hook token also opens the free-text wake and agent endpoints, prefer a small host-side relay that holds the real token and accepts only an event id from the phone. Happy to phone: a Message-trigger automation on the phone (sender is Happy, message contains a keyword) that runs a shortcut such as 'open the OpenClaw app' or 'set a Focus'; Happy sends the keyword through an in-house tool that only knows a fixed keyword list. The Mac's own shortcuts command stays under F078.
depends_on: Tailscale on the phone
gateway hooks (off by default) with a mapping per event and a dedicated tool-less events agent, or a host-side relay in front of the hook
for the reverse direction: the phone's handle on the pinned recipient list and an in-house keyword tool
caveats: Automations belong to one device and sync to other devices switched off, so each parent builds their own.

Apple lists the triggers that may run without asking (time of day, arrive, leave, CarPlay, email, message, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, NFC, charger, sound recognition and others). A Notification trigger exists but is not on that list, so it cannot be an unattended notification relay.
The hook token sits inside a shortcut on the phone, readable by anyone holding the unlocked phone.
Find My and Focus schedules already cover arrive and leave alerts. Use this where Happy adds something.
The only Shortcuts action the OpenClaw app documents is Start Live Voice, so 'tell Happy' has to go through a web request or a message.

The reverse direction is experimental. I found no Apple-documented way for a Mac to run a shortcut on another device; the keyword message is a workaround, and a phone that shares happy's Apple Account may not treat Happy's own message as incoming.

hooks.token is one shared secret for the whole hook surface. Whoever holds it can also post free text to the wake and agent endpoints for any agent in allowedAgentIds, wake text arrives as a trusted system event, and custom mappings cannot switch those two endpoints off. The allowed agent must therefore be one where injected text can do no harm.
One token means both parents' phones hold the same secret; the hook cannot tell Tony's phone from Jordan's.

Reverse direction: the Message trigger fires on any message from Happy that contains the keyword, including an ordinary reply the model was talked into writing. Use a random keyword, strip it from normal replies in a message hook, and keep the shortcut harmless.

A schedule on the gateway already covers 'pickup notes on weekday afternoons' with no phone-side setup. Phone triggers are worth it only where the phone knows something the gateway does not (in the car, at a place).
corrections.safety:
A wake is treated as a trusted system event, so nothing free-text from a phone may reach a private agent. The hook's allowed agent is a tool-less, memory-less events agent, never

-main (memory) or

-jobs (résumé plus browser); the mapping emits fixed strings chosen by event id; delivery is done by code to the owner. Hooks stay tailnet-only with their own token. For the reverse direction the keyword list is fixed in code, the sender filter is pinned, and the shortcut does only harmless things: no unlocking, no purchases, no Home scenes that touch locks or the garage.
unverified: That Get Contents of URL can send the Authorization header the hook requires. Tokens in the query string are rejected, and the Apple page I fetched documents methods and request body but not headers.

The list of Shortcuts actions for Messages, location, Focus and Home: the Apple pages I fetched cover triggers and the web-request action only.

Whether a Shortcuts action that sends a message to Happy can run unattended. If it can, the phone could trigger Happy over the existing iMessage channel, as its owner, with no gateway hook at all.

corrections.how: A cheap Android phone on a charger with the OpenClaw Android app, whose foreground service keeps the gateway connection alive. Turning on Accessibility Control in the app makes the node advertise mobile.ui.observe and mobile.ui.act (in the Android default allowlist; enabled on the phone, then approved as a pairing update). The built-in mobile_ui tool reads a semantic snapshot (text, roles, bounds) and performs one action per call; state-changing actions come back as confirmation_required until the model repeats the call with confirmed set. Give the tool to one stateless phone agent. scrcpy lets Tony watch or drive the same phone from the Mac. Pair it with the voice-node or limited profile, grant the app no Contacts, Calendar, Photos, SMS or notification access on the phone, and approve a command surface that holds only the mobile UI commands.
caveats: A second ecosystem to patch and babysit in an all-Apple house.
The docs pages mention mobile UI control only in the command-policy table. The tool is present in the installed code but has no guide page, so treat it as early.
The confirmed flag is the model confirming to itself; a real parent approval has to be added by hook.
It reads element text instead of pixels, so it is faster and steadier than iPhone Mirroring, but apps that draw custom views or mark content as secure will not be readable.

gateway.nodes.commands.deny is global. Denying callLog.search or notifications.list for this phone removes them for every node, and denying a shared command such as contacts.search would also switch it off for a parent's iPhone. Narrow this phone by what it is granted and which surface is approved, not only by the deny list.

A before_tool_call hook sees the action type and an element reference or coordinates, not the app or the label being tapped (the tool keeps the screen snapshot to itself). A parent approval prompt needs extra plumbing to say what is about to be pressed.
The built-in confirmation step looks for English keywords such as pay, send, delete and install. It is a hint to the model, not a control.
Like the iPhone app, the Android app pairs with an operator session as well as a node (see IPH-01).
For this family the school apps already notify both parents' iPhones; weekly use is unlikely to justify a second phone ecosystem.
corrections.safety: Same trifecta exposure as IPH-08. On the phone: only the target apps, no payment method, no wallet. On the gateway: keep sms.send and sms.search out of commands.allow and add them and callLog.search to commands.deny; mobile_ui only on the stateless agent; a before_tool_call hook requires a parent approval for any act other than scroll, wait or observe. The phone agent holds only mobile_ui: no nodes tool, no memory, no web, no message tool.

corrections.how: Nothing to build. Record these on the never list and enforce what can be enforced: keep sms.search, sms.send and any notification forwarding without an allowlist out of config and in gateway.nodes.commands.deny; never install banking, brokerage, payment or wallet apps on a phone an agent can drive, and delete Mail and Wallet from it (Messages and Safari cannot be deleted in the US, which is one more reason not to let an agent drive an iPhone); never remove the passcode or disable auto-lock except inside Guided Access with Touch switched off; never register Happy's number or Apple Account as a recovery or second-factor channel for a parent's account; do not sign a spare phone in to happy's Apple Account.
caveats: What iOS and OpenClaw rule out today: the iOS node has no command to read SMS, read other apps' notifications or control other apps, and computer control is marked not applicable on iOS.
iOS prohibits camera capture in the background, suspends apps shortly after they leave the foreground, and throttles background pushes without guaranteeing delivery.
An iOS app can only present a message composer for a person to approve; it cannot send an SMS on its own.
iPhone Mirroring needs the phone locked, offers no camera or microphone (so no Face ID), ends when the phone is unlocked and works with one Mac and one iPhone.
